Paper: [Amin et al. (2025), π*0.6: a VLA That Learns From Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14759).
The star distinguishes the RECAP-trained model from its supervised base model, π0.6.
RECAP stands for reinforcement learning with experience and corrections via advantage-conditioned policies.

## Problem

A robot trained on demonstrations may perform the broad steps of a task while repeating mistakes or moving inefficiently during deployment.
More expert demonstrations do not necessarily cover the difficult states that this particular policy visits.
RECAP combines demonstrations, autonomous attempts, outcome feedback, and optional human corrections to improve the policy using its actual experience. [§§I and IV](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=3).

## Previous Attempts

Imitating expert corrections supplies useful recovery actions, but corrections alone do not evaluate all autonomous behaviour or directly reward faster completion.
Policy-gradient methods are another route, although applying them efficiently to a large flow-based VLA is challenging because its action likelihood is not readily available in closed form.
RECAP instead fits a value function and uses the resulting action-quality labels as an additional condition in supervised-style policy training. [§§II and IV-B](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=4).

## Proposed Solution

The loop has three operations: collect experience, fit a value model, and train a policy conditioned on an estimated improvement indicator.
Offline pretraining applies the latter two operations to existing data.
Task specialisation adds demonstrations and then repeats the loop with newly collected robot attempts. [Algorithm 1 and §V-D](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=6).

| Data or label | Role |
|---|---|
| Pretraining data | Diverse prior demonstrations and other training tasks. |
| Task demonstrations | Initialise a specialist for the target behaviour. |
| Autonomous attempts | Reveal outcomes and states visited by deployed policies. |
| Human corrections | Supply recovery examples inside difficult rollouts. |
| Improvement indicator $I_t$ | A derived training label, recomputed using value estimates. |

The accumulated dataset includes failures as well as successes.
An indicator is not a new sensor measurement or a reward supplied by the environment at every action.
It is a label computed from experience, except where expert corrections or initial task demonstrations are explicitly assigned a positive label.
The number of demonstrations and the amount of practice differ by task; the paper does not prescribe a universal 50–100-trajectory initialisation budget. [§V-D and Appendix F](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=18).

## Reward, return, and value are different quantities

Let $o_t$ be an observation, $a_t$ an executed command, $\ell$ a task instruction, and $T$ the episode's terminal index.
The paper derives rewards from an episode-level success label:

$$
  r_t=
  \begin{cases}
  0,&t=T\text{ and success},\\
  -C_{\mathrm{fail}},&t=T\text{ and failure},\\
  -1,&t<T.
  \end{cases}
$$

The constant $C_{\mathrm{fail}}>0$ makes failure costly.
The undiscounted return from time $t$ is

$$
  R_t=\sum_{u=t}^{T}r_u.
$$

For a successful episode, this is the negative number of remaining nonterminal steps.
Consequently, faster successful completion earns a larger return.
A value estimate is an expectation of future return under the behaviour represented in the data, not the observed return from one episode or a guarantee of optimal performance. [§§III and V-C](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=7).

## A distribution over return bins

The value model predicts a categorical distribution over $B=201$ return bins, conditioned on the observation and task.
Let $b_t^*$ be the bin containing the demonstrated return and $p_\phi(b\mid o_t,\ell)$ the predicted probability of bin $b$.
The training target is a bin label, so its loss is cross-entropy:

$$
  L_V=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}
  [-\log p_\phi(b_t^*\mid o_t,\ell)].
$$

If $c_b$ is the numerical return represented by bin $b$, the scalar value used in later calculations is

$$
  V_\phi(o_t,\ell)=
  \sum_{b=1}^{B}c_b\,p_\phi(b\mid o_t,\ell).
$$

The model therefore produces a distribution first and takes its expectation when a scalar is needed.
The paper normalises returns by task length, so rewards, returns, values, and advantage thresholds must use consistent units when implementing these equations. [§IV-A and §V-C](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=4).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: what the categorical value objective estimates"}

Fix the observation and task, and let $q_b$ be the true conditional probability of each return bin in the data distribution.
Expected cross-entropy satisfies

$$
  H(q,p)=H(q)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p).
$$

The entropy $H(q)$ does not depend on the model.
The KL term is minimised at $p=q$, subject to sufficient model capacity and successful optimisation.
It is not maximised there.
Taking the expectation of the bin representatives then approximates the conditional mean return, with additional discretisation error.
This does not turn the fitted value into the optimal value of all possible policies.

The [cross-entropy note](../../study-notes/mathematics/entropy.qmd#cross-entropy) explains the classification objective, while [loss](../../study-notes/machine-learning/loss.qmd#mse) explains how scalar MSE could instead target a mean directly.

:::

## From value estimates to an improvement indicator

An advantage compares an observed continuation with the value expected at its starting state.
Write $\widehat{\mathcal A}_t$ for this scalar to distinguish it from an action chunk $A$.
For a nonterminal $N$-step continuation,

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\mathcal A}_t
  &=\sum_{u=t}^{t+N-1}r_u\\
  &\quad+V_\phi(o_{t+N},\ell)-V_\phi(o_t,\ell).
  \end{aligned}
$$

At a terminal boundary, the continuation uses the terminal outcome rather than bootstrapping beyond the episode.
The paper uses a shorter lookahead during post-training and an episode-return estimate during pretraining, rather than the same fixed $N$ in every phase. [Appendix F](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=18).

For a task-dependent threshold $\varepsilon_\ell$, the ordinary label is

$$
  I_t=\mathbf 1
  [\widehat{\mathcal A}_t>\varepsilon_\ell].
$$

Positive means above this chosen threshold according to the estimate.
It does not necessarily mean above zero, above the mean, or globally optimal.
The recipe forces human corrections to have $I_t=1$ and also uses positive labels during the initial task-specific supervised fine-tuning stage. [§IV-B and §V-D](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=5).

The paper's threshold wording is inconsistent: §V-D mentions a 30th percentile of predicted values, while Appendix F specifies selecting thresholds so that approximately 30% of pretraining demonstrations receive positive labels.
Those descriptions are not equivalent.
This note follows Appendix F's operational description, which also gives different positive fractions for post-training and some tasks; it does not assume a universal 30th-percentile rule.

## How the policy uses the label

Conceptually, the policy learns both an observation-conditioned action distribution and a distribution additionally conditioned on $I_t$.
Write $c_t=(o_t,\ell)$ for compactness.
The conceptual negative-log-likelihood objective is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  L_\pi=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[&-\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid c_t)\\
  &-\alpha\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid I_t,c_t)].
  \end{aligned}
$$

In the implemented model, discrete outputs use token cross-entropy and continuous actions use flow matching; an exact continuous-action log-likelihood is not directly evaluated.
Randomly omitting the indicator during training supplies the conditioned and unconditioned cases without requiring two explicit likelihood evaluations for every example. [§IV-B, §V-B and Appendix F](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=6).

The architecture follows [knowledge insulation](knowledge-insulation.qmd): FAST action supervision trains the backbone while the continuous expert reads its features through a stop-gradient boundary.
The low-level chunk contains joint-position and gripper commands.
It should not be described as continuous joint velocities plus a separate autoregressive gripper channel.
Textual subtask outputs are a distinct high-level prediction. [§V-A and Fig. 5](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=7).

The advantage indicator appears after the subtask text and before action outputs in the training sequence.
Thus it conditions action generation without retroactively conditioning the preceding subtask prediction.
The continuous expert cannot read the demonstrated FAST action targets. [§V-B](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=6).

## Iterative training and deployment

Deploy the current specialist, collect autonomous and corrected episodes, and add them to the task dataset.
Refit the value model on the accumulated data, obtain updated indicators, and train the next specialist.
The value model represents a changing mixture of demonstration and robot behaviour, so its estimates and labels can change as the dataset grows.
The implementation fine-tunes each iteration's value model and policy from the pretrained checkpoints, rather than necessarily continuing from the immediately previous specialist. [§V-D](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=7).

At deployment, request the positive-conditioned policy by supplying $I=1$.
This requests behaviour associated with the positive training subset; it does not force an unreliable model to choose a successful action.
The value model supplies training labels and need not be evaluated at every control step to choose that fixed input.

Classifier-free guidance is an optional further sharpening mechanism.
At the density level, define $p_0(a)=\pi_\theta(a\mid c)$ and $p_+(a)=\pi_\theta(a\mid I=1,c)$.
The paper motivates

$$
  \widehat p(a)\propto
  p_0(a)\left[\frac{p_+(a)}{p_0(a)}\right]^\beta.
$$

With $\beta=1$, this reduces to $p_+$ and direct positive-conditioned sampling suffices.
Larger $\beta$ uses a guidance construction with conditioned and unconditioned predictions.
The paper primarily tunes the training threshold and uses moderate extra guidance where useful; strong guidance is not a mandatory step for every rollout. [§IV-B and Appendix E](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=17).

## Evidence

The experiments compare supervised pretraining, offline-RL pretraining, task demonstrations, and improvement using on-robot experience.
They measure success rate and throughput on espresso making, laundry folding, and box assembly, including component ablations and longer deployment evaluations. [§VI](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=8).
These results support the full recipe in the evaluated tasks, rather than attributing every gain to a single loss term or proving monotonic improvement after every iteration.

## Limitations

Value errors, incomplete observations, imperfect corrections, and limited experience can produce misleading advantage labels.
The paper's theoretical policy-improvement motivation relies on assumptions that are not automatically satisfied by learned approximate values and practical samplers.
Conditioning on a positive label and increasing guidance therefore provide neither an optimality certificate nor a guarantee of safe actions.
Outcome annotation and real-robot data collection remain substantive parts of the method. [§VII and Appendix E](https://www.pi.website/download/pistar06.pdf#page=11).
